question_type: argmax month of a yield spread (Aa corporate minus Treasury) over a decade from one pinned issue, encoded as month*100+year

opus_path.decision: Spread = 'Aa new corporate bonds' minus 'Treasury bonds' monthly averages; window Jan 1960-Dec 1969 = 120 months; output = month*100 + year; flagged possible ties up front.
Issue is pinned (June 1970) so no vintage choice for values.
Table AY-1 'Average Yields of Treasury, Corporate and Municipal Bonds by Periods' in treasury_bulletin_1970_06.txt.

Noticed year labels were lost in OCR; counted 36 monthly rows x 4 column groups and inferred each group stacks 3 consecutive years; anchored group 4 = 1968/1969/1970 because its third block stops at May (nan after), consistent with a June 1970 issue.

Confirmed the year mapping from other printings of the same table where the year-label row survived (1970_03:4789, 1971_06), i.e. used neighbouring issues for STRUCTURE while keeping the pinned issue for values.
Parsed all 36 rows x 4 groups in a script, asserted exactly 120 in-window months, sorted spreads; top two months differ only in the second decimal, so both cells were checked.
Checked the top-two cells are identical across ~10 later issues (OCR stability).
Applied month*100+year in code, not by hand.

opus_key_moves: Treated the missing year labels as a structural problem and recovered them from another printing of the same table (1970_03:4789, 1971_06) instead of guessing from recalled yield levels
Used the cell count (36 rows x 4 groups = 12 years) and the May cut-off in the last block as internal anchors, so the parse covered the question's 1960-1969 window
Enumerated all 120 months in a script with count asserts and computed the output encoding in code

first_divergence.what_glm_did: Decided each of the 4 column groups is ONE calendar year (1966-1969), anchored only on the weekly section starting in Dec 1969; at [30] it labelled all 36 rows of group j with a single year, so the 1970 rows of group 4 (third block) were labelled 1969 and one of them became the argmax.
first_divergence.what_opus_did: Read the table as 4 groups x 3 stacked years (1959-1970), anchored by the May cut-off in the last block and by the year-label row in 1970_03:4789.
first_divergence.why_glm_went_that_way: Year labels were missing; [19] reasoned from recalled historical yield levels ('4 panels = 4 years') and ignored its own observation that there are 36 rows, not 48; [21] took the weekly-section start date as proof. At [31] it proposed 'search other bulletins for same table to see year headers' but never ran it.
first_divergence.consequence: The chosen month-year came from data outside the question window (1970 rows mislabelled 1969); the final value is far from Opus's (>25%).

secondary_errors.note: Wrote 'month*100 + year' correctly but evaluated it as digit concatenation (5-digit result); at [19] it had also mis-evaluated the same formula for another candidate. Even the right month would have been encoded wrong.
Hand-typed the table as a Python literal: duplicated a panel and filled nan cells with invented values; noticed at [23] and replaced by a programmatic parse at [30].
Resolved the conflict between the question's 1960-1969 window and its 4-year reading by doubting the question, not its parse.

text_vs_mechanism: Mechanism needed. All three arms saw that a 4-year reading conflicted with the question's 1960-1969 range and blamed the question. The prompt arm already had a generic 'count the extracted cells' step and a two-panel-OCR lesson for another table, and still miscounted rows and computed nothing. The cards arm rejected other issues because the question pins June 1970. A label-recovery tool plus a period-map check would catch the structural error. The encoding error, which hit all three arms, is cheapest to catch with an output-transform/range check.
notes: Two failures stack here: (1) a flattened table whose period labels were lost in OCR, and (2) a question-specified output encoding that every arm evaluated wrongly: two concatenated the month digit with the year, one wrote the year first. The none arm computed the spreads in Python but still evaluated the encoding by hand; the other two arms computed nothing in code. The idea 'the question pins issue X, so I may not look at other issues' blocked the cheapest fix (reading the label row from another printing); harness text should separate 'source of values' from 'source of structure'. A STATE index of table layouts (AY-1: 4 groups x 3 stacked years, anchor years via a labelled vintage) would help later AY-1 questions. The prompt learner produced exactly such a lesson after this postmortem (L-ay1-year-trio-panels).
